analysis.one_liner: Bans the herbicide atrazine — its use, production, sale, and import — to keep it out of water.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in October 2024 with three cosponsors, referred to the House Agriculture Committee, and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would immediately and permanently cancel every federal registration of the weed killer atrazine, ban its sale or use including leftover stocks, bar any future registration, revoke the legal limits on atrazine residue in food within six months, and block emergency exemptions. The bill's stated purpose is to stop a pesticide that the text says is among the most commonly detected in the nation's drinking water, groundwater, and streams, and which the European Union banned more than two decades ago.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water from farm-country wells, streams, and public systems — especially farmworkers and rural residents — would face less exposure to a chemical the bill text links to elevated cancer risk, birth defects, and reproductive harm. Wildlife, particularly amphibians and endangered species, would also be spared: the bill text cites EPA's 2022 finding that atrazine is likely to adversely affect 1,013 threatened or endangered species.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural residents, farmworkers, and water drinkers

how_it_helps.text: It cancels all atrazine registrations by operation of law the day it is enacted, rather than leaving the decision to the EPA's slower administrative process.
It revokes food-residue tolerances within six months and prohibits sale of existing stocks, so the chemical exits use and commerce quickly rather than lingering for years.

The bill text cites a USDA estimate that a ban would cut corn yields only 1.19%, and notes that Italy and Germany saw no yield drops after banning atrazine in 1991, suggesting farm costs of a ban are modest.

analysis.who_pays: Atrazine manufacturers lose a product representing roughly 80 million pounds of annual U.S. use, and corn and other row-crop farmers lose a low-cost, widely used weed-control tool, facing substitution costs the bill text puts at roughly a one percent corn yield reduction.

drawbacks.text: Farmers would lose one of the cheapest and most widely used herbicides on corn and other crops; even the USDA's modest 1.19% yield-loss estimate applies to corn alone, and growers would bear switching costs not compensated by the bill.

The ban takes effect immediately with no phase-out period and prohibits even sale of existing stocks, giving distributors, retailers, and growers no runway to use up or return product already in the supply chain.

By canceling atrazine by operation of law, the bill bypasses the EPA's own scientific review process, which some would argue should weigh current data rather than have Congress fix the outcome in statute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits reach a very wide public — cleaner drinking water, less farmworker exposure, and protection for over a thousand endangered species — while the costs fall on a narrow set of manufacturers and on farmers facing roughly a one percent corn yield reduction by the government's own estimate. A fair criticism is design, not direction: an immediate cancellation with no phase-out for existing stocks is abrupt, and a scheduled wind-down would have eased the transition for growers. On the whole, the public health and environmental gains outweigh the concentrated, modest costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, but the committee never took it up, and the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill with three Democratic cosponsors on October 11, 2024, in the final weeks of the 118th Congress.
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee, which referred it further to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology on November 4, 2024.
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Atrazine manufacturers and distributors keep selling roughly 80 million pounds a year, and growers keep using it; the water contamination, farmworker exposure, and harm to endangered species the bill targeted continue under existing EPA rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Atrazine manufacturers and its farm users

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ban Atrazine Toxicants Act on October 11, 2024.

for.name: Reps. James McGovern, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Alma Adams
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no additional members joined afterward.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology, and never held a markup or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and the bill went to a Republican-run committee that never acted, so no vote ever revealed where either party stood.

industries.note: Atrazine is the nation's second-most used herbicide at roughly 80 million pounds a year, and the bill would erase that entire market by immediate cancellation with no future registrations. Keeping the product on the market means its makers' interest runs directly against the water-quality and health interests of the surrounding public.

Growers lose a cheap, broad-spectrum weed control tool the USDA estimates accounts for about a 1.19% corn yield reduction if banned; farmers opposing the ban have an economic stake that sits against the public's interest in cleaner water, though they are cost-bearers rather than profiteers.
The prohibition on selling even existing stocks would strand inventory and cut a product line from the supply chain with no phase-out period.
